title: Luke 23:44–56
context: Darkness falls, the temple veil is torn, and Jesus commits his spirit to the Father and dies. The centurion confesses him righteous, the crowds go home grieving, and Joseph of Arimathea buries him while the women watch. Both traditions see Jesus’ trusting death and real burial as central to the gospel.

verses.text: It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.
verses.arminianNotes: Darkness covers the land from noon to three. Arminian readers see a sign of judgment and cosmic grief at the death of the Son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a sign of judgment, recalling Amos 8:9. Both agree Luke presents the darkness as meaningful, not merely atmospheric.

verses.text: The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn in two.
verses.arminianNotes: The sun is darkened and the temple veil torn. Arminian readers see access to God opened through Jesus’ death (Hebrews 10:19–20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the torn veil the same way, and some also see judgment on the old order. Both agree the way into God’s presence is now through Christ.

verses.text: Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” Having said this, he breathed his last.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus cries, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” quoting Psalm 31:5. Arminian readers see trusting surrender, a model for believers in death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same trust and note that Jesus gives up his life rather than having it taken from him in defeat. Both find comfort here for dying believers.

verses.text: When the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying, “Certainly this was a righteous man.”
verses.arminianNotes: The centurion glorifies God, calling Jesus a righteous man. Arminian readers note that a Gentile soldier responds rightly to what he sees.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the final human verdict at the cross confirms Jesus’ innocence, and that a Gentile glorifies God, anticipating the mission to the nations.

verses.text: All the multitudes that came together to see this, when they saw the things that were done, returned home beating their chests.
verses.arminianNotes: The crowds go home beating their chests. Arminian readers see the beginnings of remorse that could lead to repentance (Acts 2:37).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same sign of grief. Both note that sorrow is a beginning, not yet full repentance.

verses.text: All his acquaintances and the women who followed with him from Galilee stood at a distance, watching these things.
verses.arminianNotes: His acquaintances and the women stand at a distance watching. Arminian readers note the faithfulness of the women who stayed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these become witnesses of the death and burial, important for the resurrection testimony. Both honor the women’s steadfastness.

verses.text: Behold, there was a man named Joseph, who was a member of the council, a good and righteous man
verses.arminianNotes: Joseph, a council member, is good and righteous. Arminian readers note that not every leader consented; individual choices mattered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note God raising up a faithful man in an unlikely place. Both appreciate Luke’s fair portrait of a dissenting council member.

verses.text: (he had not consented to their counsel and deed), from Arimathaea, a city of the Jews, who was also waiting for God’s Kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes: He had not consented to the council’s decision and was waiting for God’s Kingdom. Arminian readers see a man whose expectant faith shaped his action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same godly expectation, like Simeon and Anna (Luke 2). Both see him as among the faithful remnant.

verses.text: This man went to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body.
verses.arminianNotes: Joseph asks Pilate for Jesus’ body. Arminian readers note the courage it took to identify with a condemned man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same courage. Both see his request as an act of love and public allegiance.

verses.text: He took it down and wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb that was cut in stone, where no one had ever been laid.
verses.arminianNotes: He wraps the body and lays it in a new rock-cut tomb. Arminian readers stress that Jesus truly died and was truly buried.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the same reality of death and burial, part of the gospel Paul received (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The new tomb also helps identify the place later found empty.

verses.text: It was the day of the Preparation, and the Sabbath was drawing near.
verses.arminianNotes: It was the Day of Preparation, with the Sabbath approaching. Arminian readers note the time pressure that shapes the burial.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same. Both observe that the Sabbath rest sets up the first-day discovery in chapter 24.

verses.text: The women who had come with him out of Galilee followed after, and saw the tomb and how his body was laid.
verses.arminianNotes: The women follow and see the tomb and how the body was laid. Arminian readers note that they know exactly where he was buried.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same: their later testimony rests on accurate observation, not confusion.

verses.text: They returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
verses.arminianNotes: They prepare spices and rest on the Sabbath according to the commandment. Arminian readers see devoted, law-keeping disciples who expect to anoint a dead body.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that their faithfulness to the commandment and their preparations show they were not expecting resurrection, which makes their later witness more striking.
